content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper studies semantic parsing for long context. The datasets used here are recipe datasets: the model targets to generate executable recipe plans given the description. The paper studies the problem in a few shot learning setting.

To tackle this issue, the paper notices that there are prediconditions that exist in the dataset (e.g. mix the egg assumes that eggs are already prepared). The paper leverages such information in inference by 1) incorporating such information in ranking score function 2) propose an algorithm that can insert into the generated plan so that these conditions are satisfied. 

Using these information, the paper shows improvement in generating better plans.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The paper found again some general preconditions and should be leveraged
- The paper proposes two methods to leverage these preconditions and show improvements

Weakness:
- (Suspect) if the subject is about the precondition, one seems to be able to evaluate such criteria partially (e.g. before mix egg also check is egg is already prepared). Not taking account the algorithmic complexity, checking every time during generation steps guarantees that such problem can be alleviated. I am not sure what I miss here.
- There are significant amount of work leveraging generation consistency (or logical form consistency) that the paper mentioned none of them. Just to give some examples, https://aclanthology.org/P16-1127.pdf guarantees that the generation contains no syntactic error; https://aclanthology.org/D17-1160.pdf guarantees type consistency. There are also other works that incorporate general, fuzzy logics. The paper mentions and leverages none of those.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper exposes clear motivation. To solve the reicpe semantic parsing tasks, the paper notices some general prior knowledge to leverage and derives two techniques to improve performance. Those techniques are well exposed although those techniques do not seem new given the abundant litterature in the field.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposed a method for few-shot semantic parsing of instructional texts. The core idea is to (1) leverage large language models to learn parsers from small amounts of training data (few-shot learning); (2) employ planning methods and domain information to rand and correct candidate parses from the decoding. The core idea of the second step (and the contribution of this paper) is *Planning Augmented Semantic Parsing*, which leverages a formal symbolic planning representation to rank and correct candidate plans. The experimental results on recipe interpretation in two cooking domains have shown the effectiveness of the methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- This method is simple and requires no modification to the neural model architecture.
- The experimental results show the effectiveness of the methods.
- The excerpted examples provide an in-depth ablation study for the advantage of planning.

Weakness
- Only test on cooking recipe interpretation. This method is very limited to a certain types of semantic parsing tasks, where an explicit definition for planning in the domain is required.
- The design of the planning is not clear, especially regarding how to refine the syntax error score and precondition error score.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I cannot see so much novelty based on the current paper draft. First, the steps of learning parsers from small amounts of training data are based on the recent progress of large pre-trained language models, which is the typical prompt training process. Second, the reranking and planning rely on domain knowledge engineering for each instructional text, and there is no surprise this method can improve the baseline results since you import extra knowledge to complement the limited knowledge learned from few-shot training.
content.summary_of_the_review:
- The methods work effectively on the two cooking interpretation datasets. However, the results are within our expectations since the reranking and planning process introduces specific domain knowledge information to complement the limited knowledge learned from the few-shot training. In this case, it should be compared to the fine-tuning settings to see if we can reduce the training cost by incorporating symbolic knowledge.
- Also this method seems to work only on a limited type of semantic parsing tasks, where the definition of planning is clear. However, what about some semantic parsing tasks which require more structural information in the output space? e.g., graph-based semantic parsing or code generation.
- The structure of Section 4 is a little bit confusing. Does the order of each subsection correlate to the order of Figure 1? Why talk about the planning domain before prompt design? It seems that the latter part is within the LLM parsing module. A reorganization of Section 4 is highly recommended.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for mapping length instructional text (recipes) to executable abstract actions (e.g., preheating an oven). The main contribution is a (1) re-ranking method for generated programs and (2) a planner that inserts steps for unsatisfied preconditions. They evaluate on recipe domains from Tasse and Smith 2008, and Bollini et al. 2013.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Studies an important problem of mapping long-form instructions to executable representations.

Weaknesses:
- There are long-standing approaches in semantic parsing to produce programs that are guaranteed to be semantically and syntactically correct. This includes constrained decoding (e.g., Krishnamurthy et al. 2017), grammar-based decoding (Yin and Neubig 2017), and intermediate output spaces that guarantee executable programs when mapped to the target language (e.g., for SQL generation; Guo et al. 2019). None of these approaches are evaluated in this paper, and instead the proposed contribution is to simply re-rank (rather than reject, which would be the simplest approach to guaranteeing executability) generated candidate programs.
- As an example, ~25% of generated are syntactically incorrect in Table 3. This is a huge proportion of examples, and the proposed method doesn't provide guarantees against generating such examples, while existing methods in semantic parsing do. One might argue that these existing methods require engineering intermediate output spaces or grammars for decoding, but if the domain-specific language exists and is executable, that grammar should already be available, and worst case one could check executability at inference time (which is already happening in the proposed method) and reject inexecutable programs.
- The intuition in Eq 1 is confusing, maybe because the notation is underspecified. Is the goal to map a given training example to a test example that most closely matches it, or the other way around? I am not sure what the purpose of this equation is for (perhaps because the inference method is somewhat unclear).
- Inserting steps to satisfy preconditions is an interesting approach; however, it's unclear how this method accounts for required parameters in the inserted steps. How does this method (Alg 1) ensure that the precondition is met correctly, e.g., that the oven is preheated to a specific temperature?
- Why not evaluate execution accuracy, i.e., whether the chosen program results in the correct world state? (I assume there is some kind of environment for executing programs, if preconditions can be checked automatically).
- I had a different conclusion to these results than the paper suggests at the end: this is not really showing the benefit of neurosymbolic methods, since the results don't address the problem of executability; rather, they are showing the failure of these large language-to-code models to generate executable code in a few-shot setting.

Small comments:
- Citations appear to be broken
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
- Paper is relatively easy to follow. I would suggest having more examples of STRIPS-style functions as well as how the preconditions are defined in both datasets.

Quality:
- The experiments seem relatively thorough, though the metrics are not well-justified (execution accuracy is missing). I'd also be interested in seeing how random+plan or rank(PPL)+plan works; i.e., choosing a random plan and inserting steps to satisfy preconditions.

Novelty:
- The proposed method is not exactly new; perhaps this particular re-ranking (and the planner that satisfies preconditions) is new, but there are many existing approaches to semantic parsing that provide actual guarantees on the executability and validity of generated programs.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method shows some improvements over not reranking and not inserting steps, but there are too many open questions (e.g., how to guarantee the planner inserts steps that have the correct parameters, like temperature), and no comparison to existing methods in semantic parsing that actually guarantee valid output programs. If the paper were reframed as a critical and thorough study of the failures of large pretrained text-to-code models (this would require significant reworking of the paper and experiments as well), it could be interesting, but as it stands it's unclear what this paper adds to existing semantic parsing literature.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors developed a method for few-shot semantic parsing of instructional texts. The system takes long-form instructional texts as input and produces sequences of actions in a formal language that enable execution of the instructions. The authors try to leverage the fact that valid semantic parses also require sequences of steps that constitute an executable plan. The experiment setting is in few-shot learning by prompting existing large pretrained language models. Most novelty is during decoding, the proposed method employs planning methods and domain information to rank and correct candidate parses. The authors experimented with two recipe interpretation tasks. The authors show that utilizing planning domain information improves the quality of generated plans.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The authors proposes a easy to understand and pluggable method to existing large language models that could improve the semantic parsing results by reranking.
2. The authors' proposed method is tested in few-shot learning setting, which is an efficient way of domain adaptation, and achieves better results, showcasing the effectiveness of the method.

Weaknesses:

1. The authors experiment the proposed methods on two datasets, but both are cooking recipe datasets and has similar domain language for semantic parsing. With the overall goal of improving semantic parsing as mentioned in the title, it is important to showcase how the method could benefit multiple more diverse domains with domain knowledge. The dataset is also small, even for an evaluation dataset, with only 260 and 60 examples respectively. This experiment limits the confidence of the generalizability of such method, as the method requires domain knowledge and thus it is very crucial to test the domain generalizability. Some example domains to test includes text-to-SQL, text-to-Python, Geo, ATIS, or other knowledge base question answering database

2. Some related work should be mentioned for more discussion about the novelty and comparison with the work. Some lines of work includes constrained decoding and execution guided decoding of the autoregressive generation in semantic parsing, e.g. SeaD: End-to-end Text-to-SQL Generation with Schema-aware Denoising, Synchromesh: Reliable code generation from pre-trained language models,  PICARD - Parsing Incrementally for Constrained Auto-Regressive Decoding from Language Models, etc.

3. The method should also be compared with some reranking work in the line of semantic parsing, e.g. Reranking for Neural Semantic Parsing
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The presentation, clarity is very good.
The novelty is average and limited to a small audience of the whole semantic parsing domain.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a simple and effective method but only proves it useful on two small cooking datasets, that does not prove generalizability to other domains in semantic parsing and it may not fully transferrable because we do not know the effort required related to domain knowledge.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
